title: India restored 21.76 mn ha Land during 2011–2020, generating 1.22 bn person-days of Employment: Shri Bhupender Yadav at UNCCD COP17 in Ulaanbaatar, Mongolia
subtitle: Land Restoration is India's established National Priority, integral to Sustainable Land Management, Biodiversity Conservation, Climate Action and Rural Development: Union Environment Minister
body_text:
Union Minister for Environment, Forest and Climate Change Shri Bhupender Yadav today said that land restoration is an established national priority for India and is integral to the country’s efforts on sustainable land management, biodiversity conservation, climate action and rural development. Speaking at a side event organised by the IUCN at the 17th Conference of the Parties (CoP 17) to the United Nations Convention to Combat Desertification (UNCCD) in Ulaanbaatar, Mongolia, Shri Yadav said India views restoration not as a standalone intervention, but as an essential component of sustainable and resilient development.
The Minister said India is among the major global pledgers to the Bonn Challenge. In 2015, India made an initial commitment to restore degraded and deforested land, which was subsequently enhanced to 26 million hectares by 2030. He said this commitment reflects both the scale of the challenge and India’s confidence in its national capacity to deliver restoration at scale.
Shri Yadav said India has recently released its Second Progress Report on the Bonn Challenge, covering the period 2011–2020. During this period, 21.76 million hectares were brought under restoration, supported by significant convergent financial flows and generating approximately 1.22 billion person-days of employment, he said. The Minister said these figures demonstrate that restoration can deliver both environmental and socio-economic outcomes by reviving degraded landscapes while creating employment and supporting rural livelihoods. Importantly, he said, the assessment goes beyond measuring hectares. It captures restoration across forests, agriculture, soil and water conservation and other land-use systems, recognising that restoration must respond to the ecological and socio-economic characteristics of each landscape.
The reporting process has also highlighted the need to further strengthen systems for monitoring restoration outcomes, financial flows and livelihood impacts, Shri Yadav said. India is therefore undertaking the next reporting cycle for 2021–2025, in collaboration with the ICFRE Centre of Excellence on Sustainable Land Management and IUCN. This cycle will focus on three key dimensions – area restored, financial flows and employment generated – while strengthening the national evidence base for restoration. The Minister said the credibility of any commitment ultimately rests on implementation. India has therefore developed a multi-sectoral and landscape-based approach to translating this ambition into action.
The Green India Mission, Shri Yadav informed, is strengthening forest and tree cover, ecosystem services and climate resilience. Through the Compensatory Afforestation Fund Management and Planning Authority, substantial resources are being directed towards compensatory afforestation and allied restoration activities. The Nagar Van Yojana for urban greening extends the restoration agenda to urban and peri-urban landscapes through urban forestry and green spaces. These efforts are complemented by watershed development, agroforestry, soil and water conservation and community-based restoration across the country, the Minister said.
Shri Yadav stated that this experience demonstrates that restoration cannot be delivered through a single programme or sector. It requires convergence across landscapes, sectors and levels of governance – from local communities and States to the Union Government. Looking beyond 2030, the Minister said India’s objective must be not only to restore more land, but to restore better, finance better and deliver measurable and lasting outcomes.The Minister  said this will require innovative financing mechanisms to mobilise greater public and private investment; stronger regional and international partnerships to share knowledge, technologies and experience; and sustained participation of local communities. Restoration is ultimately sustained by the people who depend upon and manage these landscapes, the Minister added.
Shri Yadav concluded by stating that India remains committed to working with international partners to advance restoration at scale. India’s experience demonstrates that ambitious commitments can be translated into measurable outcomes when supported by strong institutions, sustained financing, sound science, robust monitoring and partnerships across sectors and levels of governance. He said India looks forward to working with all partners in advancing this shared agenda.

ministry.name: Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change

enrichment.summary: At UNCCD COP17 in Ulaanbaatar, Mongolia, Union Environment Minister Bhupender Yadav stated that India restored 21.76 million hectares of degraded land between 2011-2020, generating about 1.22 billion person-days of employment, as per India's Second Progress Report on the Bonn Challenge. India had pledged to restore 26 million hectares by 2030 under the Bonn Challenge, enhanced from its 2015 commitment. The Minister outlined India's multi-sectoral approach including the Green India Mission, Compensatory Afforestation Fund Management and Planning Authority (CAMPA), and Nagar Van Yojana, and announced the next reporting cycle for 2021-2025 in collaboration with ICFRE and IUCN.
enrichment.context:
The Bonn Challenge is a global voluntary effort launched in 2011 to restore 150 million hectares of degraded and deforested land by 2020 and 350 million hectares by 2030, aligned with the UNCCD's Land Degradation Neutrality target and the Aichi Biodiversity Targets. India joined the Bonn Challenge in 2015 with an initial pledge of 13 million hectares, later enhanced to 26 million hectares by 2030 - among the largest national pledges globally. This restoration agenda is delivered through a mix of programmes: the Green India Mission (one of the eight missions under the National Action Plan on Climate Change), CAMPA (which channels funds collected for diverting forest land to non-forest use into compensatory afforestation), and the Nagar Van Yojana for urban forestry.

The UNCCD, one of the three Rio Conventions (alongside UNFCCC and CBD), addresses desertification, land degradation and drought, and its Conference of Parties (COP) is held biennially - COP17 in Mongolia continues India's active engagement following its hosting of COP14 in New Delhi in 2019. India's reporting on land restoration outcomes, including employment and financial flows, feeds into international assessments of progress toward Land Degradation Neutrality (SDG target 15.3) and demonstrates the socio-economic co-benefits of ecological restoration, particularly for rural livelihoods.

prelims_questions.question: The 'Bonn Challenge', often mentioned in the news, is related to which of the following?
options: Global commitment to restore degraded and deforested land
Global target to reduce carbon emissions from aviation
International agreement on marine plastic pollution
Global framework for phasing out fossil fuel subsidies
prelims_questions.explanation: The Bonn Challenge is a global voluntary effort launched in 2011 aiming to restore 150 million hectares of degraded land by 2020 and 350 million hectares by 2030; India has pledged to restore 26 million hectares by 2030 under it.

prelims_questions.question: The United Nations Convention to Combat Desertification (UNCCD) is one of the three Rio Conventions. Which are the other two?
prelims_questions.explanation: The three Rio Conventions emerging from the 1992 Rio Earth Summit are the UNFCCC (climate change), CBD (biological diversity), and UNCCD (desertification).

mains_questions.question: India has pledged to restore 26 million hectares of degraded land by 2030 under the Bonn Challenge. Discuss the significance of land restoration for India's climate, biodiversity and rural development goals, and examine the institutional mechanisms in place to achieve this target.

Land degradation and desertification pose significant challenges to India's ecological and economic security. Critically evaluate the effectiveness of programmes like the Green India Mission and CAMPA in addressing this challenge.

study_notes.reason: The release carries a solid factual core (Bonn Challenge targets, India's pledge figures, CAMPA/Green India Mission institutional details) alongside genuine analytical material on India's multi-sectoral restoration strategy, socio-economic co-benefits and financing/monitoring gaps, making it genuinely dual-use rather than one-sided.

prelims.point: Bonn Challenge: launched in 2011 as a voluntary global effort to restore 150 million hectares of degraded/deforested land by 2020 and 350 million hectares by 2030.
prelims.why_important: UPSC frequently tests global environmental pledges/targets and their launch years alongside national commitments.

prelims.point: India joined the Bonn Challenge in 2015 with an initial pledge (13 million hectares), later enhanced to restore 26 million hectares of degraded land by 2030 — among the largest national pledges globally.
prelims.why_important: India's specific numerical pledge under a global commitment is a classic factual detail examiners use to test scheme/target recall.

prelims.point: CAMPA (Compensatory Afforestation Fund Management and Planning Authority) channels funds collected for diversion of forest land to non-forest use into compensatory afforestation and allied restoration activities.
prelims.why_important: Tests understanding of the compensatory afforestation mechanism and the institution managing it, often confused with other forestry funds.

prelims.point: UNCCD is one of the three Rio Conventions, alongside UNFCCC and CBD, addressing desertification, land degradation and drought.
prelims.why_important: A recurring prelims distinction — identifying which convention deals with which environmental issue among the Rio trio.

mains.point: India's restoration agenda relies on a multi-sectoral, landscape-based convergence approach (Green India Mission, CAMPA, Nagar Van Yojana, watershed development, agroforestry) rather than a single programme.
mains.analytical_use: Useful for questions on how India operationalises large-scale environmental commitments through institutional convergence across sectors and levels of governance.

mains.point: Restoration efforts generated significant employment (1.22 billion person-days), illustrating socio-economic co-benefits of ecological restoration for rural livelihoods.
mains.analytical_use: Supports answers on synergies between environmental restoration and rural employment/livelihood generation.

mains.point: The Minister flagged the need for stronger monitoring systems and innovative financing mechanisms to mobilise public-private investment for restoration beyond 2030.
mains.analytical_use: Relevant for 'discuss challenges in implementation of India's climate/land commitments' type questions, highlighting financing and monitoring gaps.

both.concept: India's Bonn Challenge pledge and progress reporting (26 million hectares by 2030; 21.76 million hectares restored 2011-2020 per Second Progress Report)
both.prelims_angle: Could be tested as factual data — pledge figures, reporting periods, and the name/scope of the progress report.
both.mains_angle: Allows analysis of the gap between ambitious international pledges and actual on-ground delivery, and the credibility of voluntary global commitments when backed by institutions and financing.

low_priority.point: Minister's rhetorical framing of 'restore better, finance better' and calls for 'sustained partnerships'
low_priority.reason: Generic ministerial rhetoric without specific policy content or measurable commitment.

low_priority.point: Concluding remarks on India's commitment to work with international partners
low_priority.reason: Ceremonial closing statement carrying no new factual or analytical content.
